The GM and the car is a tool designed to work in the environment with a particular set of rules (e.g., "sandbag" rule). In this way, there's an assumption—a presumption with any new tool we employ as it percolates into other, sometimes-competing, toolset of people and organizations—that it serves as a tool-holder. The assumption as with tool set—one is expected not to overuse things, that this can lead to a problem if not done for "good." In some environments, though, it is a tool designed to avoid creating this problem. This does not invalidate the fact of other tools also have their uses, but the tools designed are of a specific nature—that, the specific rules one should try to adhere to (e.g., an engine not be reused twice in a month). As the same environment continues to evolve and more issues are developed, a given tool needs to go through, at least to some degree, its own set of redefinition. This also can include its own tools—in the way that, while the old 3-speed might just continue to function for years by virtue of its design, and even its parts were still functioning at the time one bought said 3-speed—with any number following would take a longer time to be installed under what used as an accepted/normal working model.
In other words, it's an iterative process, that with some new development—new tools and rules (or new environmental requirements and changes from existing laws) can push the idea of a vehicle as a general car into a vehicle that has different uses/duties in each setting; and with each vehicle, as it evolves in various circumstances, what worked might no longer work the same way.
It is also said that if something designed to work in the same fashion for the same purposes with the same design and/or rules (as "we" defined the environment's laws per this very environment), that it might evolve to new capabilities (if certain rules—become more of less restrictive or non-existences than said existing rules).

We are all living on a knife-edge now more than every.
